likely: Respiratory viruses (a substantial proportion of exacerbations are viral, not bacterial)
possible: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (in severe COPD with frequent exacerbations, prior isolation, or recent hospitalization)
pathogens.why: When a bacterial component is present, the same three organisms responsible for most bacterial bronchitis/sinusitis are implicated. A substantial fraction of COPD exacerbations are triggered by viral infection alone, which is why purulent sputum (rather than dyspnea or sputum volume alone) is the best clinical indicator of likely bacterial involvement justifying antibiotics.

clinicalPearls: An exacerbation is defined clinically as an episodic acute worsening of respiratory symptoms (increased dyspnea, cough, and/or a change in sputum volume and character), usually evolving over fewer than 14 days; it may or may not be accompanied by fever, myalgias, or sore throat (p.2301).

COPD exacerbation is a clinical diagnosis; no single test confirms it, and measurement of pulmonary function (unlike in asthma) has not been shown to aid diagnosis or management of a COPD exacerbation (p.2301).

The strongest single predictor of future exacerbations is a history of a previous exacerbation, and the single greatest risk factor for hospitalization is a history of a previous hospitalization (p.2301).

The cardinal symptoms of a bacterial exacerbation are increased cough with increased sputum production, sputum purulence, and increased dyspnea relative to baseline; nontypeable H. influenzae exacerbations typically show only low-grade fever and no infiltrate on chest x-ray (p.1305-1307).

Exacerbation frequency rises as airflow obstruction worsens: patients with severe obstruction (FEV1 <50% predicted) average 1-3 episodes per year, though some severely obstructed patients are not frequent exacerbators (p.2301).

A target oxygen saturation of 88-92% is used; in patients with acute or chronic hypercarbia, supplemental O2 does not reduce minute ventilation but may modestly raise arterial PCO2 by altering ventilation-perfusion relationships - this should not deter giving the oxygen needed to correct hypoxemia (p.2302).
harrison.pathophysiology: A variety of stimuli converge on a final common pathway of airway inflammation with increased respiratory symptoms. Viral respiratory infection, once thought less common than bacterial infection, is detected by PCR-based studies in over half of exacerbations; acquisition of a new bacterial strain is associated with increased near-term exacerbation risk. Non-infective contributors include air pollution, allergens, and environmental/Aspergillus sensitization, and in a significant minority no specific precipitant is identified (p.1756, p.2301).
infectionMimics: Pneumonia - the most frequent abnormal finding on chest imaging in this setting; about 25% of x-rays obtained for moderate-to-severe exacerbations in severe COPD are abnormal (p.2301).
nonInfectiousMimics: Pulmonary embolism - should be actively considered because the incidence of PE is increased during COPD exacerbations (p.2301).
Congestive heart failure - a common alternative or contributing finding on imaging in patients presenting as an exacerbation (p.2301).
Pneumothorax - asymmetry on chest examination may indicate pneumothorax (or large-airway obstruction) mimicking an exacerbation (p.2301).
additionalInvestigations: Arterial blood gas in patients with advanced COPD, a history of hypercarbia, altered mental status (confusion, sleepiness), or significant distress; hypercarbia is defined as PCO2 >45 mmHg and carries treatment implications (p.2301).
Chest x-ray or chest CT in patients with severe underlying COPD, moderate-to-severe distress, or focal examination findings (p.2301).

C-reactive protein, as part of emerging expert-consensus objective criteria (combining dyspnea, vital signs, CRP, and arterial blood gases) to diagnose and stage exacerbation severity, mainly of use in the emergency department (p.2301-2302).
redFlags: Respiratory acidosis with hypercarbia (PCO2 >45 mmHg, pH <=7.35) - an indication for noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation, which reduces mortality, need for intubation, complications, and length of stay (p.2302).

Severe respiratory distress, severe hypercarbia and/or acidosis despite noninvasive ventilation, markedly impaired mental status, respiratory arrest, or hemodynamic instability - indications for invasive mechanical ventilation via endotracheal tube (p.2302).
New or worsening hypoxemia, severe underlying COPD, or significant comorbidity such as heart failure - features suggesting the need for inpatient treatment (p.2301).

Inability to speak in complete sentences, accessory muscle use, perioral or peripheral cyanosis, tachypnea, tachycardia, altered mental status, or paradoxical abdominal wall motion on examination (p.2301).
harrison.prognosis: Mortality for patients requiring mechanical ventilatory support during a COPD exacerbation is 17-49% for that hospitalization. After any hospitalization for COPD, about 20% are rehospitalized within 30 days and 45% within a year, and mortality is approximately 20% in the year after discharge. Because of the high mortality of invasive ventilation, advance directives (e.g., resuscitation preferences) should be discussed in the outpatient setting (p.2302).
pitfalls: Withholding needed supplemental oxygen for fear of CO2 retention is an error; oxygen should be titrated to 88-92% saturation to correct hypoxemia despite a possible modest PCO2 rise (p.2302).

Contraindications to noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation that must be screened for include cardiovascular instability, impaired mental status, inability to cooperate, copious or unclearable secretions, and craniofacial abnormality or trauma preventing mask fit (p.2302).
M. catarrhalis is easily mistaken for commensal Neisseria species on respiratory culture and was historically overlooked as a pathogen, so culture interpretation requires care (p.1308).
harrison.severityClassification: Assessment should grade both the severity of the acute exacerbation and the severity of preexisting COPD; the more severe either component, the greater the likelihood of needing hospital admission. An expert consensus has proposed more objective criteria to diagnose and stage exacerbation severity using dyspnea, vital signs, C-reactive protein, and arterial blood gases, although this schema is more useful in the emergency department than the outpatient setting (p.2301-2302).
